sections.title: Prerequisite Review: Determinants as Area
sections.content: Briefly define the determinant of a 2x2 matrix as the 'signed area' of a parallelogram formed by two vectors (column vectors of the matrix). Explain that the sign indicates orientation.
sections.example: Vectors u=(2,0) and v=(0,2) form a square with area 4. The determinant |A| = 4.

sections.title: Visualizing the Linear System
sections.content: Represent the system Ax = b as a vector combination: x(a1) + y(a2) = b, where a1, a2 are column vectors. Show how the solution (x, y) represents scaling factors for these basis vectors.
sections.example: A robot arm needs to reach point b(5,5). It uses two motors represented by vectors a1(1,0) and a2(0,1). The system solves how much to scale each motor.

sections.title: Geometric Derivation of Cramer's Rule
sections.content: Explain that replacing a column of A with b creates a new parallelogram. Show that the ratio of the area of this new parallelogram to the original |A| equals the scaling factor of the missing vector.
sections.example: For x*a1 + y*a2 = b, the area of the parallelogram formed by (b, a2) is exactly x times the area of (a1, a2). Thus, x = det(b, a2) / det(a1, a2).

sections.title: Summary and Intuition
sections.content: Consolidate the concept: Cramer's rule is simply an area-ratio calculation. It tells us how much 'space' the vector b occupies relative to the transformation defined by matrix A.
sections.example: A chef balancing two ingredient vectors (a1, a2) to hit a target nutrient profile (b). Cramer's rule finds the exact 'weight' of each ingredient via geometric scaling.
